catalog_quote: 1.4.3. Stress 1.4.3.1. General rule The stress position is determined by following one general rule. See below as for exceptional cases. (1) In polysyllabic words, the stress falls on ǝCC or VC85 (not syllable but a mere sequence of phonemes) nearest the end of the word. čəllámč "I learnt", ma kəčbátš "she did not write" saknin "living (pl.)", yəčkássər "it (m.) is broken", ykəčbúli "they write to me", ... yáfəm (<*yáfhəm) "he understands", ... kəčbú (<*kəčbúh) "they wrote it (m.)". (2) Monosyllabic words (free morphemes) always bear the stress. ... But bound morphemes, e.g. ma "(negative particle)", qa "(preverb for the present)", ša "what?" do not bear the stress. ... [fn. 85: C may be historical h.] ... 1.4.3.2. Exceptional cases Following are the exceptional cases of the stress rule formulated above. 1.4.3.2.1 ... All perfect verbs of the 3.m. have ultimate stress, e.g. təbbáh "he called, čġəddá "he had lunch", fəršák "he relaxed" etc. REMARK But in the imperfect and imperative the stress falls on the penultimate syllable (see 1.4.3.2.3.(1a) below). tábbəh "call (m.)!", čġádda "have lunch (m.)!" etc. 1.4.3.2.2. Nouns etc. (1) Dissyllabic feminine nouns ... functioning as adjectives on the following patterns bear the stress on the ultimate syllable. (a) CəCCá. To this pattern belong (a) Nouns denoting colours or physical defects (< CA CaCCā) ' urá "one-eyed (f.)" (m. wər) ... (b) CCuCá. ... As far as I have observed, only these two nouns on this pattern are attested.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress goes on the vowel of the rightmost 'heavy' sequence in the word: the last əCC (schwa + two consonants) or VC (full/long vowel a, i, u + consonant); a word-final long vowel with no following consonant does not attract stress (ykəčbúli), and the rule is stated over phoneme strings, not syllables (historically *h counts: yáfəm < *yáfhəm, kəčbú < *kəčbúh). Monosyllabic content words are stressed; proclitics ma (neg.), qa (present preverb), ša 'what?' are unstressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress in the recovered text of sec. 1.4.3.
new_statements.exceptions: (i) All 3rd-masc. perfect verbs (derived/quadriliteral, e.g. təbbáh 'he called', čġəddá 'he had lunch', fəršák 'he relaxed') have ultimate stress, whereas the corresponding imperfect/imperative has penultimate stress (tábbəh 'call!', čġádda 'have lunch!'); (ii) disyllabic feminine nouns/adjectives of pattern CəCCá (colours and defects < CA CaCCāʾ, e.g. ʿurá 'one-eyed') are stressed on the ultima; (iii) sec. 1.4.3.2.3: stress has a phonemic function in broad areas of the morphology, e.g. nəkčáb 'it is written' (VII) vs nákčəb 'I write' (I), nəqčál vs náqčəl, and a 3msg pronoun suffix on a vowel-final monosyllable is marked only by stress (loss of *-h).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word including proclitics/enclitics (ma kəčbátš 'she did not write' is treated as one stress domain; clitics themselves unstressed). In Yoda's transcription a, i, u are the long vowels (written without macron) and ə the only short vowel, so 'VC' = long vowel + C; footnote 85 qualifying 'VC' was not visible. Text recovered from overlapping Google Books scanned snippets, not from page scan; wording should be checked against the print pages 111-113.
new_statements.identity_note: Yoda 2005 describes 'TJ', the Arabic dialect of the Jews of Tripoli city (speakers recorded in Israel, emigrated 1949-52 and 1967) = jude1264 / ISO yud exactly. D'Anna 2021 (not obtained) describes the Yefren (Jebel Nafusa) Jewish variety, which he treats as a separate 'Yefreni type' within Libyan Judeo-Arabic; Glottolog files it under the same languoid.

sources.note: Theoretical paper on schwa placement in nouns/verbs/adjectives (own fieldwork, one speaker b. Tripoli 1947, ~5000 items). All forms carry stress marks (e.g. [Srə́b] 'he drank', [Sə́rbu], [ʕáfəlkətʃ]) but no stress rule is stated; defers to Yoda 2005 as the description of record.

sources.note: Orthography and style of written Libyan Judaeo-Arabic; only a passing mention (p. 181) of the general Maghribi deletion of unstressed short vowels in open syllables. No stress rule for the dialect.

sources.note: Transcribed texts with notes on the vowel system (long a i u, single short vowel ə; etymological h realised as ɦ). No stress rule; acute accent written only on a few final-stressed forms (e.g. čqəṛṛə́ḅ).
